title: Architecture reviews
description: Learn how to evaluate system designs, spot risks early, and guide your team toward architectures that scale with the business.

data.text: An architecture review is not a chance to enforce your favorite patterns. It is a structured conversation about whether a design will hold up under real-world conditions: growth, failure, changing requirements, and limited team capacity. As a senior engineer, you bring the experience to ask the hard questions before the team invests months of work.
The best architecture reviews feel collaborative, not adversarial. The goal is to strengthen the proposal, not to prove the author wrong.

items: Scalability: Can this design handle ten times the current load?
Reliability: What happens when one service, database, or region fails?
Maintainability: Can a new team member understand and modify this system?
Cost: Does the infrastructure budget align with the expected traffic and growth?
Security: Are sensitive data and access patterns properly protected?
Timeline: Is the proposed approach achievable within the available time and skills?

data.text: Questions are more powerful than statements in an architecture review. Instead of saying 'this will not scale,' ask 'what happens when traffic doubles?' That invites the author to walk you through their reasoning rather than becoming defensive.

items: What is the expected load in one year, and how does this design handle it?
What is the single point of failure in this system?
How will we debug this in production when something goes wrong?
What assumptions are we making about data consistency?
Can we simplify this without losing the core benefits?

data.text: Architecture reviews often fall into predictable traps. Recognizing them early keeps the conversation productive.

rows: Designing for imagined future scale that may never arrive
Start simple, leave clear extension points
Choosing technology to look good rather than to solve the problem
Match the tool to the actual requirements
Set a deadline and accept 'good enough for now'
Defending an existing design because of past investment
Evaluate the current design on its own merits

data.title: Watch out for complexity creep
data.text: Complexity is not free. Every new service, queue, or abstraction adds operational overhead. If the team does not have experience running it, that complexity becomes a hidden risk.

data.title: Key takeaways
data.text: Great architecture reviews ask questions instead of handing down judgments. Focus on scalability, reliability, and team fit. Flag anti-patterns early, and always weigh complexity against the team's ability to operate the system.
